newsitem.title: BRAZIL: US officials seek "positive" trade dispute outcome.
newsitem.headline: US officials seek "positive" trade dispute outcome.

text.p: One day after Brazilian officials reacted with surprise, even indignation, to the prospect of U.S. trade sanctions, American officals in the Brazilian capital said they hoped to find a constructive, positive solution that would avoid any high-volume confrontation over Brazil's auto industry policy.

U.S. diplomatic sources Wednesday said the start of a probe under Section 301 of U.S. trade law announced Tuesday by acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, did not necessarily signal a U.S. determination to slap retaliatory measures on Brazil.

"We think we have a good constructive relationship with Brazil and if there is a way to reach a constructive, positive solution rather than bashing each other over the head, we think that would be better," said a U.S. source, requesting anonymity.

Section 301 of the U.S. trade law allows retaliations against unfair trade practice after a 90-day period of consultation and investigation into the charges of unfair trade practices brought by U.S. manufacturers.
In her announcement Tuesday, Barshefsly said Australia and Indonesia, along with Brazil, would face investigations for unfair auto trade practices.
Washington finds two elements of Brazil's auto policy, known as the Car Industry Regime, as especially contentious.

One is a clause allowing car makers to import at a preferential 35 percent tariff as long as they export a similar quantity. Both General Motors Corp and Ford Motor Co are major players in Brazil and Chrysler Corp recently announced investment plans.
The other is a 60 percent national contents stipulation, which has enraged U.S. car parts manufacturers and labor unions.
On Tuesday, Brazil's Minister of Industry and Commerce, Francisco Dornelles, reacted with outrage at the U.S. decision to probe charges that Brazil was an unfair trader in the motor vehicle arena.
"The rules (on auto industry policy) won't be altered," he told the Gazeta Mercantil daily while on the municipal campaign trail in Rio de Janeiro for his Brazilian Progressive Party.
Washington places a high importance on its own motor vehicle industry, however for reasons including the fact that it accounts for one out of every 10 jobs in durable goods manufacturing.

"In light of the importance of the U.S. auto industry to the U.S. economy, eliminating foreign barriers to U.S. exports of autos and auto parts is of vital importance to the industry's economic growth and to U.S. national economic interests," Barshefsky said.
Other Brazilian officials who reacted with surprise to the announcement preferred to take a more conciliatory approach than Brazilian Industry and Commerce Minister.

Jose Alfredo Graca Lima, head of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's economics department, rejected the U.S. contention that Brazilian car industry policy hurt America's car exports, but noted that behind the rhetoric the U.S. position dealt with specifics that could form the basis for dialogue.
"I note there is no indisposition to consult (on the part of the Americans or of Brazil)," Graca Lima said.
The Section 301 probe runs parallel to formal World Trade Organization consultations over the car rules, which set lower tariffs for manufacturers with a Brazilian base.
Washington could demand WTO panel arbitration after October 8, but any formal WTO ruling would likely take up to two years.

"The issue of principle remains. However, I think there is a realization now that the WTO process is time-consuming and that there are definite negative effects on (U.S. car and car part) exports now," the U.S. source said.

The rules were also challenged within the WTO by Japan, South Korea and the European Union but Brazilian officials said those disputes had all but fizzled out since Brasilia offered them quotas for low-tariff imports.
Japan could have requested a WTO panel as of Monday. "But I don't think they will," said Graca Lima, head of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's economics department.
Whether Brazil could assuage U.S. grievances through widening its low-tariff quotas to include the United States was speculative, Graca Lima said.
It was too early to tell if something similar could resolve the dispute, he added.
-- Brasilia newsroom 55-61-2230358
